prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators and their experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells and in three-dimensional bismuth-based crystals

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep topological insulators as my preferred single-part prize, and my configuration is unchanged: Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan. The reason is the one I care most about, a clue from nature that confirmed a sharp idea. The Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state were predicted, and the quantized edge conductance in HgTe (2007) and the surface states of Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 seen by ARPES (2008-2009) are direct observations that nature could have refused. About two decades of independent confirmation across transport, ARPES, STM and many material families make the interpretation stable, and members on both sides of the clock debate agree on that maturity. The chair's question on the 2016 prize has a concrete answer in my view: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz rewarded topological invariants in quantum Hall states and phase transitions in model systems, while this is time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials without a magnetic field, a distinct discovery with its own experimental proof. I would word the citation to the prediction and the two experimental discoveries so that it is explicit about what is honoured and does not claim the whole topological-materials field. Round 1 did move me on one thing. I no longer treat BAO as something to push, since only Pearce and I ever saw it, and I accept that the names do not map cleanly onto the achievement.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the real weakness and I do not want to hide it. Mele is the painful omission: he co-wrote the 2005 Kane-Mele papers, and a prize that names Kane without him says something about who originated the Z2 insulator. Swapping Hasan for Mele would repair the theory side but leave the three-dimensional discovery unrecognised, and the 3D theory itself was shared among Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Roy, which is a harder allocation than the 2D one. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who told Molenkamp what to measure, remain outside any three-name cut, and Zhang cannot be credited. The novelty question relative to 2016 is answerable but needs to be argued in the citation. If the committee judges that the third seat cannot be defended, a cleaner configuration exists elsewhere, and I would then look at twisted bilayer graphene or, for the cleanest credit, the clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig moved Mele into his trio in place of Hasan, arguing that Kane and Mele are inseparable on the mechanism and that the 3D credit is diffuse among theorists outside the list.
responses.response: I take the argument about the 3D theory seriously: Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Roy all contributed, so the 3D credit cannot be allocated on the theory side. But that is a reason to credit the 3D discovery through the experiment that settled it, not a reason to drop it. Hasan's ARPES work is the observation that turned a prediction into a material anyone could measure, and with Mele in his place the prize would be a two-dimensional theory-plus-transport prize and would overlook the part with the broadest materials impact. Your trio gives the cleanest pairing of the original theory and is a respectable alternative; mine gives the cleanest pairing of prediction and observation. I have not moved, but I would not call your configuration wrong, and a citation worded around the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation would serve both.

responses.point: Olsson makes her support conditional on a check of what each 2005 paper contributed and on whether Mele has an independent claim, and she says that if the credit cannot be settled B017 is her next choice.
responses.response: Your condition is the right one, and I share the unease. The two 2005 papers, the graphene one and the Z2 one, were written together, and what they give us is a joint classification. Even so, I do not think the committee can credit the 2D theory to Kane alone and justify it from the papers; what justifies three names is that the Nobel rule forces a choice, and the choice should follow the discoveries confirmed in nature. That is Molenkamp for the first observation and Hasan for the first 3D observation, with Kane as the theorist whose prediction both tested. I would ask the committee to record openly that Mele is an equal originator of the Kane-Mele model in the 2005 papers and is omitted only by the three-person limit, so that the citation does not imply otherwise. If your check shows that the Z2 paper is substantially Mele's idea, I would want to hear it, and that would move me toward Mehlig's trio.

responses.point: Lindroth says that if the committee insists on a discovery, the strongest honest case for lattice clocks is the observation of relativistic time dilation across a millimetre, and she would centre the citation there rather than on constants or dark matter.
responses.response: That is a better argument than the one I answered in round 1, and I want to credit it. A redshift measured across a millimetre in a many-atom system is a positive observation and a genuine test of general relativity at a new scale, and it is the kind of clue from nature I asked for. It narrows my objection but does not remove it. It is still a demonstration of what the instrument can resolve, and it confirms a prediction that nobody doubts. A topological insulator is a new class of matter. I would also note that the many-body control that gives you the millimetre result is Ye's contribution, while Katori's contribution is the magic wavelength, so a citation centred on the redshift risks changing which of the two names carries the weight. I keep the clocks as a strong second tier and have moved it up in my private list since I no longer hold that the null results alone are the whole payoff.

responses.point: Kroll replies that parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea from the 2005 and 2012 tools, and that limits on constants and ultralight dark matter are information about nature.
responses.response: I accept the first part: the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle, not just the comb or ion control in a different place, and that answers the overlap worry better than I allowed. I also accept that a bound with a stated uncertainty is a measurement. Where we still differ is on what a Nobel citation rewards. If the redefinition of the second happens, or a clock sees a signal, I will move quickly, and I said so in round 1. Until then the case rests on capability, and I find a new class of matter confirmed in the laboratory a stronger discovery. I would not oppose B047 if the committee prefers the cleaner credit, and the two-name Katori and Ye attribution is genuinely better than anything in B006. I just do not think that cleanliness should outweigh the scientific case.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks whether the committee prefers B006 with the widest ballot support but an unresolved third name, or B047 with narrower support but a clean credit, and he asks whether lattice clocks look incremental after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I would answer your question this way: I do not count ballots in place of science, and breadth of support does not by itself decide it for me. B006 wins for me on the discovery, because it is a new phase of matter proven by experiment, and it also happens to have the most settled trio across the proposals, six of seven naming Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan in the shortlist data. The unresolved third seat is a real cost, but it is a cost of crediting a discovery made by a community, not a sign that the discovery is uncertain. On your incrementalism worry, I think the lattice concept is distinct enough to answer it, which is why B047 is my second alternative, but a citation would still have to be written carefully. I also note that you disclosed that you are a supporter of B047, and I would not discount your view for it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene because the prediction was quantitative, the 2018 experiment could have failed, and many groups have reproduced it, and he asks whether open pairing physics is a maturity problem.
responses.response: I ranked B017 third and I like the logic: Bistritzer and MacDonald made a prediction with a number in it and nature agreed. My difficulty is timing, the same as Olsson and Mehlig raise. The existence of flat bands and of correlated insulators is well reproduced, but the superconductivity is the headline and its origin is unsettled, and the credit among Cao, Dean, Jarillo-Herrero and the earlier flat-band theorists has not been worked out. Big ideas can take a long time to prove their worth, and here we do not yet know whether the moire family will be what you think it is. I would not call that a maturity problem for the discovery of flat bands, but I would for a citation that must mention the superconducting state. If B006 fails on credit, B017 is where I would go next, and it stays my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Hasan rather than Mele as the third name, and whether Mehlig and Olsson's check of the 2005 papers shows that Mele's claim is stronger than I have argued.
Whether the 2016 prize is seen as leaving enough room for the Z2 topological insulator, and whether my wording of the citation is enough to make the distinction.
Whether the open Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit can be handled in the wording alone, given that Zhang is deceased.
Whether the redefinition of the second or a clock-based signal will arrive soon enough to change my view of B047.
I am a string theorist and not an experimentalist in condensed matter or atomic physics, and I rely on colleagues and outside experts for the experimental credit details.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no known personal or institutional connection to Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan, Mele, Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates. My supervisor David Gross and the Uppsala string group are unrelated to this shortlist, and my dark-energy work is only thematically close to the baryon acoustic oscillation candidate, which I no longer prefer. I note the disclosures from Johansson, Kroll, Olsson and Pearce and have no objection to their participation as long as they are discounted openly.
